structure.title: Book I · Testing a judgment against a case
structure.text: Two generals show clemency for quite different reasons. A paid tutor must decide whether a child has understood a lesson. A traveller reports customs that horrify a European audience. Montaigne tries each example from several positions, including the uncomfortable one occupied by the person delivering the verdict.

structure.title: Book II · How much can the judge know?
structure.text: The long defence of Raimond Sebond makes human confidence itself a subject. Examples from animals trouble our claims to a unique command of reason. Around that argument sit shorter essays on books, cruelty and family resemblance in which the examiner's own peculiar habits keep entering the evidence.

structure.title: Book III · Experience close to home
structure.text: An essay nominally about coaches can reach the European conquest of America. The closing essay on experience returns to how a particular aging man eats, sleeps and bears pain. His own body is the subject about which he has most information and remarkably little final certainty.

people.name: Montaigne
people.text: The same reader of ancient history is also an estate owner, a bereaved friend, a former magistrate and a man with kidney stones. Each position gives him grounds for challenging a claim that seemed entirely persuasive from another.

people.name: Étienne de La Boétie
people.text: The essay on friendship has someone particular to remember. Its efforts to account for their attachment disclose how little a list of admirable qualities can explain why this person became indispensable to that person.

context.title: An essay as an attempt
context.text: A title supplies a starting point. A remembered saying can prompt a story whose details change the question the writer thought he had set himself. One can enter through education, friendship or a bodily complaint and discover the same restless intelligence already at work.

notice.why: The first case can tempt us into a general rule. The next may lead to the opposite result through recognisably similar behaviour. Montaigne is interested in what sort of judgment remains possible after both stories have had their say.

notice.text: Catch a quotation meeting a private habit.
notice.why: An ancient author may offer an imposing maxim about death or courage. A memory of illness, a fall from a horse or an admission about appetite gives Montaigne a way to measure what that maxim is worth on an ordinary day.

opening: Montaigne sits down to write about friendship, fear, education, or some odd thing he has read, and sooner or later finds himself implicated. His memory fails, his body interrupts, and his behaviour refuses to match the dignity of his opinions. The essays have the freedom of a conversation with someone too curious to keep up a flawless appearance. A minor observation can lead into a major uncertainty, and the writer's willingness to revise himself makes his company more trustworthy than a performance of certainty would be.
